props.title: Rat Scratch Fever

sections.content: **Rat Scratch Fever (2011)** (2011) represents one of those gloriously unhinged B-movie creature features that knows exactly what it is. Following in the footsteps of mutant rat classics like Willard (1971) and Food of the Gods (1976), this direct-to-video romp delivers exactly what genre fans crave - practical effects, over-the-top gore, and entertainingly hammy performances. The film's plot about genetically enhanced lab rats escaping into a small town echoes similar scientific-experiment-gone-wrong narratives like Deep Blue Sea (1999) and **Piranha 3D** (2010).

sections.content: The early 2010s saw a resurgence of deliberately campy creature features, with **Sharknado** (2013) leading the charge into self-aware territory. **Rat Scratch Fever** (2011) sits comfortably in this tradition, though it maintains slightly more serious horror elements than its successors. Director Steve Latshaw, known for low-budget gems like **Jack-O** (1995), brings his signature blend of practical effects and tongue-in-cheek humor to the proceedings.

The film's practical rat effects, while clearly operating on a limited budget, show impressive creativity in an era increasingly dominated by cheap CGI. This approach aligns it more with classic creature features like Rats: Night of Terror (1984) and Of Unknown Origin (1983) than contemporary digital-heavy productions. The decision to use real rats for many scenes, supplemented by practical puppets for the mutated specimens, grounds the film in tangible horror despite its B-movie trappings. sections.content: The killer rat subgenre has a rich history in horror cinema, from the psychological terror of **Ben** (1972) to the ecological horror of **Deadly Eyes** (1982). **Rat Scratch Fever** (2011) distinguishes itself by combining elements of both approaches - the rats are both physically threatening and unnaturally intelligent. This hybrid approach would later influence films like **Mulberry Street** (2006), which uses rat-human mutations as a metaphor for urban decay.
